items.title: Design and simulation of an interactive human robot disassembly system for end of life phones
items.summary: Introduction With the growing challenge of e-waste and end-of-life phones, a clear demand is required for efficient and scalable recycling solutions. This study proposes a simulation-based and proof-of-concept framework for a collaborative robotic disassembly system that consists of six specialized stations designed to support the systematic extraction and routing of the main end-of-life phone components. The main contribution is the joint integration of a flexible architecture, more than 20 operational and collaborative constraints, and multimodal voice–gesture interaction for dynamic task reassignment and error recovery. Methods This study integrates human-robot collaboration (HRC) and human-robot interaction (HRI) using voice and gesture commands to enable adaptive task reassignment and real-time error correction with reduced downtime. This framework combines simulation-based evaluation, RoboDK modeling, constraint-driven simulation, and HRC scenarios to assess system responsiveness. Over 30 operational and collaborative constraints were mathematically formulated. Results The Constraint-Driven Python simulation produced an average cumulative processing time of 955.37 s for a modeled batch of 10 phones over 200 iterations, corresponding to an average simulated processing time of 95.54 s per phone, with error rates ranging from 3.3% to 4.1%. items.title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
items.summary: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLORE, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.

items.title: Differentiable Contact Dynamics for Legged Locomotion: Policy Learning and Contact-Implicit Trajectory Optimization
items.summary: This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes. The proposed gradient replaces this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the de Saxcé-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and less than 2 min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients
